quote: Stanford lists Li as inaugural Sequoia Professor of Computer Science, founding co-director of HAI, former SAIL director, former Google Cloud AI/ML chief scientist, and co-founder/CEO of World Labs.

Li earned a Princeton physics BA with high honors in 1999 and a Caltech electrical engineering PhD in 2005; her current work spans computer vision, robot learning, spatial intelligence, and ambient healthcare intelligence.
In May 2026 Stanford named James Landay HAI director; Li moved to a university-wide senior advisor role on AI to the president and co-chair of the HAI advisory council with John Hennessy.
Li states that she was born in Beijing, spent her first sixteen years in Chengdu, immigrated to the United States, and conducted Tibetan medicine research in Tibet in 1999-2000.

The Stanford-hosted CV records a BA in physics from Princeton, certificates in applied/computational mathematics and engineering physics, an EE master's and PhD from Caltech, and a dissertation on visual recognition.
The CV records faculty appointments at UIUC, Princeton, and Stanford, including SAIL leadership from 2013 to 2018.
Princeton reports that Li immigrated during high school and regularly returned from college to help run her family's dry-cleaning business in Parsippany, New Jersey.

Stanford HAI describes her family arriving in New Jersey with very little money, her learning English while working in restaurants and the family dry cleaner, and her receiving a full scholarship to Princeton.
Li recalled that her family opened the dry cleaner during her first college year and that she operated it on weekends for seven years while acting as the primary English-speaking family member.

Li's 2005 dissertation, advised by Pietro Perona and Christof Koch, combined computational models and human psychophysics across attention, natural scenes, one/few-shot object recognition, and unsupervised scene categorization.
Li explained that Caltech let her bridge computer vision with neuroscience through work with Pietro Perona and Christof Koch, shaping a human-centered view of AI.
The 2009 ImageNet paper presented a WordNet-organized image database; at publication it contained 12 subtrees, 5,247 synsets, and 3.2 million images, built at scale with Amazon Mechanical Turk.
The ILSVRC paper documents annual large-scale image recognition challenges beginning in 2010, involving millions of images, hundreds of categories, and participation by more than fifty institutions.
AlexNet trained a deep convolutional neural network on roughly 1.3 million ImageNet images across 1,000 classes; this was separate algorithmic and systems work by Krizhevsky, Sutskever, and Hinton.
Li and colleagues proposed a Bayesian approach that transfers learned priors across object categories, allowing informative recognition from one or a few examples and evaluating it on 101 categories.
The 2002 study tested rapid natural-scene categorization under severely limited attention, connecting human visual psychophysics with computational recognition.
Karpathy and Li linked image regions and natural-language sentence fragments with convolutional and recurrent networks, advancing image-text retrieval and description generation.
Visual Genome introduced dense scene annotations for 108,077 images, treating objects, attributes, relationships, region descriptions, and questions as grounded links between vision and language.

The 2020 Nature review described contactless sensing and machine learning for healthcare workflows, patient safety, and independent aging, while emphasizing privacy, validation, and transparency challenges.
Stanford launched HAI in 2019 under John Etchemendy and Fei-Fei Li, with a mission spanning research, education, policy, and practice to improve the human condition.
The Stanford program began as SAILORS in 2015 for underrepresented high-school students and later became Stanford AI4ALL, co-founded and co-directed by Li, Olga Russakovsky, and Rick Sommer.
In 2023 Senate testimony, Li advocated demystifying AI, privacy and fairness safeguards, transparent public procurement, and sustained public investment in AI research.
The ImageNet team reported fairness and representation problems in the people subtree, identified 1,593 unsafe synsets, and removed 600,040 associated images while restricting access.
The fairness paper proposed filtering non-imageable or offensive people categories and rebalancing demographics in the ImageNet people subtree.
Crawford and Paglen argued that large training datasets embed political and social judgments, challenging the idea that image labels or person categories can be neutral.
World Labs says Li co-founded the company with Justin Johnson, Christoph Lassner, and Ben Mildenhall to build models that perceive, generate, reason about, and interact with 3D worlds.
World Labs announced in February 2026 that it had raised one billion dollars in new funding from investors including AMD, Autodesk, NVIDIA, and others.
World Labs introduced Marble as a multimodal world model that generates editable 3D worlds from text, images, video, or coarse 3D inputs and can export multiple representations.
The 2025 Queen Elizabeth Prize recognized Li alongside six other pioneers for contributions to modern machine learning, including high-quality datasets and benchmarks.
The 2024 VinFuture Grand Prize recognized Li, Yoshua Bengio, Geoffrey Hinton, Jensen Huang, and Yann LeCun for foundational contributions to neural networks and deep learning.
Google's 2018 Cloud AutoML announcement presented Li's role in making custom machine-learning systems accessible to organizations with limited AI expertise.
Google stated in 2018 that it would not pursue follow-on Project Maven contracts and would apply its AI principles to future cloud work, while continuing non-weaponized government collaboration.
Li's 2023 memoir recounts her immigrant family experience, scientific formation, ImageNet, and her argument for human-centered AI.
A 2023 interview described Li's immigration around age fifteen and emphasized her concern with present harms such as bias, misinformation, surveillance, and unequal power.
